How to use the cluster well

Six habits, each with the number from this page that justifies it. The two at the top are worth more than everything else combined.

1

If your job can checkpoint, submit to a *_requeue partition

The same H100 costs 418 per GPU-hour there against 2649 on kempner_h100. Identical hardware — you are paying for the right not to be interrupted.

6.3× cheaper

2

No cross-GPU communication? Ask for kempner_rtx

Sweeps, one seed per GPU, eval fleets and data generation never touch the interconnect. It is the cheapest dedicated partition and holds more memory per card than the 80 GiB parts. Gradient sync (DDP, FSDP, ZeRO) is the exception — those nodes reach a neighbour at only 53 GB/s.

96 GiB per card

3

Hours you burn now slow everyone's queue later

There is no hard GPU-hour budget here; the cost is fairshare. ydu_lab has drawn 2.5× its slice, so new jobs from the whole account queue behind lighter users.

2.5× our share

4

Check the quota, never df

df reports the whole shared array and says everything is fine while we sit at our own ceiling. Ours: quota -g ydu_lab /n/lab_storage/ydu_lab — 2.0 TiB left. Every allocation also has a separate file-count limit.

98% full

5

/n/netscratch is scratch, not storage

Files there are deleted after 90 days and are not backed up. Keep only what can be regenerated or re-downloaded; a directory has vanished from under this lab before.

90-day purge

6

Request the cores you will use, and use the GPU you hold

Job Defense Shield mails the lab when a job takes 4 cores and uses 1, or holds a GPU at 0% utilisation. Both waste fairshare that everyone shares. jobstats <jobid> shows what a job actually used.

FASRC emails you

Storage

Quota is per lab group per filesystem — df shows the whole shared array and will tell you everything is fine while the lab is at its ceiling. Each allocation has two independent limits, space and file count, and hitting either one fails writes while the other still looks fine. Space is the binding constraint everywhere here.

Who is using each quota

One table per quota card above, in the same order, counting the owner of each file — wherever it sits and whoever's directory it is in, so a shared dataset bills to whoever uploaded it, as the filesystem does. A group quota (netscratch, holylabs) counts that group's files; a directory's own allocation (lab_storage) counts everything inside it. Walked by us: /n/holylabs/LABS/kempner_ydu_lab/Everyone, /n/holylabs/LABS/kempner_ydu_lab/Lab, /n/holylabs/LABS/ydu_lab/Everyone, /n/holylabs/LABS/ydu_lab/Lab, /n/lab_storage/ydu_lab, /n/netscratch/ydu_lab/Everyone, /n/netscratch/ydu_lab/Lab. Private folders cannot be read, so tables can come in under the quota. Also inside these trees, billed to other labs' groups — /n/holylabs: sitanc_lab 15.8 GiB, glassman_lab 7.6 GiB, dam_lab 5.8 GiB; /n/netscratch: rcai_lab 1.4 TiB, sham_lab 661 GiB, kempner_sham_lab 560 GiB, dam_lab 621 MiB, glassman_lab 43.4 MiB, shieber_lab 40.5 MiB, hankyang_lab 15.3 MiB, 575666864 385 KiB.

Folders the scan can't read

33,576 private folders, 70 owners. Their files still count against the quotas above but can't be attributed to anyone, which is most of why the tables come in under the cards. Each line is one of the owner's folders and how many private folders sit inside it; running chmod -R g+rX <folder> on that one folder opens all of them (every folder above it needs g+x too). A folder inside a private folder can't be seen at all, so opening one can reveal more. Some trees hold more than the 500 private folders recorded per directory walked; another 122,849 are counted but not listed. Summary CSV · every path (CSV, gzipped).

Compute

There is no hard GPU-hour budget on Cannon — the lab's cost is fairshare. Hours burned now push the whole account's priority down for everyone later, which is what makes this table worth reading together.

Account standing

32,516 GPU-hours last 7 days · 105,769 last 30

AccountGPU-hours 7dGPU-hours 30d SharesUsageStanding
ydu_lab 9,083 31,781 1.18% 3.00% 2.5x share

Standing = effective usage ÷ normalized shares. Above 1x the account has drawn more than its slice and new jobs queue behind lighter users.

How fast each card is, and what it suits

no prices here — capability only. Vendor specs, with measured values on this cluster in grey where we have them

CardVRAM GiB bf16 TFLOP/smeasured Memory GB/sCard-to-card
H200 141 990 4,800 NVLink
H100 80GB 80 990 640 (65%) 3,350 NVLink
RTX PRO 6000 96 503 396 (79%) 1,792 PCIe — 53 GB/s measured
A100 40GB 40 312 1,555 NVLink
A100 80GB 80 312 2,039 NVLink
If you are running…limited by ask forwhy
Sweeps, seeds, eval or inference fleets, data generation nothing shared — each GPU runs its own job RTX PRO 6000 No weights cross between cards, so the interconnect never matters and the only question is throughput per card.
Single-GPU training, model comfortably fits raw compute H100 / H200 Twice the bf16 throughput of the RTX and nearly three times an A100's.
Model, batch or context does not fit in 80 GiB VRAM H200, then RTX PRO 6000 141 GiB and 96 GiB are the only options above 80; the RTX is the cheaper of the two by a wide margin.
Autoregressive generation / LLM decoding memory bandwidth, not compute H200 Decoding re-reads the weights every token, so 4,800 GB/s is worth more here than peak FLOPs. The RTX is the weakest card on this axis.
Multi-GPU with gradient sync — DDP, FSDP, ZeRO, tensor parallel the interconnect anything with NVLink Avoid the RTX nodes: measured 53 GB/s card-to-card, PCIe speed and 27× slower than a card reaching its own memory.
Fine-tuning a small model, or debugging queue time, not the card whatever is idle A 40 GiB A100 on a requeue partition starts sooner and costs least; the card is rarely the limit while you are still finding bugs.

The first question is not which card — it is whether your job can be preempted. The same H100 costs 6.3× more on kempner_h100 than on gpu_requeue — identical hardware, the whole difference is whether your job can be interrupted. If it checkpoints, a *_requeue partition is the cheapest GPU on the cluster and still reaches H100s and H200s.

If you cannot be preempted, then card choice matters, and kempner_rtx is the value pick among the dedicated partitions: cheapest of them, and 96 GiB per card fits models the 80 GiB parts cannot. The tradeoff is the interconnect — measured here, an RTX card reaches its neighbour at only 53 GB/s, PCIe speed and 27× slower than reaching its own memory. So anything that synchronises every step (DDP, FSDP, ZeRO, tensor parallelism) can lose more to communication than it saves.
Most of what this lab runs does not synchronise at all. A hyperparameter sweep, one seed per GPU, an eval or inference fleet, a data-generation rollout — each GPU minds its own work, nothing crosses the interconnect, and more cards for the same fairshare is simply more throughput.

No one here matches that name.

A GPU-hour is one GPU held for one hour — 8 GPUs for 3 hours is 24 of them. It measures time allocated, not work done: a GPU idling at 0% bills exactly the same as one running flat out, which is what the cluster's idle-GPU warnings are about. Two windows are shown because they say different things — a big 7-day number inside a similar 30-day number is someone who just started, while a 30-day number spread evenly is a steady long-running load.
